narrative:
Based on the assessment, the model estimates a 12% chance that you will fail your final year. While this may seem low, the school's policy requires additional support for any student whose risk reaches 10% or above, which is why you are being asked to complete remedial courses.

Interestingly, the three factors that most influenced this prediction all actually worked in your favour, pushing toward passing rather than failing — yet their combined effect was not quite enough to bring your risk below the threshold.

The most influential factor was your record of past academic failures, of which you have none. This is a strong positive signal, matching the average among students who are not required to take remedial courses, and it meaningfully reduced your predicted risk. The second most important factor was your reason for choosing this school, which was its reputation. This also nudged the prediction toward passing, suggesting that students who make deliberate, reputation-based school choices tend to perform better. Finally, the quality of your family relationships, which you rated as good, similarly contributed to a lower predicted risk.

Despite all three of these factors working in your favour, your overall profile — including elements such as your very high frequency of going out with friends, which stands out compared to most peers not in remedial courses where medium levels are most common — means your risk remains just above the school's safety threshold.

You should treat the remedial courses as a precautionary opportunity. Reflecting on how you balance social activities with study time could make a meaningful difference in securing a successful final year.
